title: MCP Server
markdown:
Open Executive can run **as an MCP server**, the inverse of the MCP *gateway* (which lets the Executive consume external MCP servers). The server exposes Open Executive's company-grounded context and its specialist council to external MCP clients — Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, or any other agent — so they can ground themselves in *this* company and pull domain analysis **inside their own loop**, without re-explaining anything.

The value is structured, attachable context, on-demand specialist analysis, and the person's own Executive turns (ask, answer a card, run a workflow) from the AI app they already use.

## Transport & mount

The server speaks **Streamable-HTTP** and is mounted into the existing FastAPI app at `/mcp` (built with the `FastMCP` SDK, `streamable_http_path="/"` mounted under `/mcp` so the endpoint is exactly `/mcp`). Mounting a sub-app does not run its lifespan, so the API lifespan runs `mcp.session_manager.run()` for the life of the process — without it every `/mcp` request would fail. The module lives at `openexecutive/mcp_server/` and is wired in `api/main.py`.

## Auth

The `/mcp` endpoint is **not** exempt from the shared-secret middleware, so it is gated like the rest of the API: clients send `x-api-key: $BACKEND_SHARED_SECRET`. One tool also needs a credential of its own: `post_progress_update` takes a per-source token in the `x-source-token` header (see below), on top of the gate, never instead of it. FastMCP's DNS-rebinding (Host-header) check is disabled because the endpoint authenticates with a header secret rather than a cookie — a browser rebinding attack cannot supply the key — and traffic arrives through the deployment's TLS terminator.

## Who is asking

Every handler answers as the caller the API already verified. The mounted app shares the outer request's state, so what `caller_gate` decided reaches the handler through FastMCP's request context, and `api.caller.person_id_for` resolves the person by the same rule as the web chat:

| Caller | Asks as |
|---|---|
| Open mode, no `x-caller-email` (direct use, local) | the principal |
| Open mode with `x-caller-email`, or a signed-in person (`x-caller-assertion`) | that person; no one when they are not on the roster |
| Operator (signed local login) | the principal |
| Service (signed callers on, only the shared secret) | no one, never the principal |

A deployment that fronts `/mcp` with its own sign-in and stamps the signed caller, as the UI proxy does, therefore gets per-person answers with the web app's rules.

## Resources (read-only context)

Pure reads, no LLM calls. Each resource calls the web app's own route function with the MCP request (`mcp_server._through_route`), so it shows exactly what that person sees on the web, and a route's refusal comes back as the JSON-RPC error message.

| Resource URI | Contents | Who may read it |
|---|---|---|
| `oe://company/profile` | Structured company profile, as a prompt block | anyone |
| `oe://departments/state` | Each department's mission, scope, lead and people by name (names only for someone on the roster), check-in, what it watches, goals, and its Approvals level by name (Careful, Balanced or Hands-off) | anyone |
| `oe://today/briefing` | Today's brief, built as `GET /today` builds it for them | someone on the roster |
| `oe://cards/needs-you` | The Needs you cards waiting on the caller | someone on the roster |
| `oe://today/done-for-you` | What the Executive did for them | as the Done for you route |
| `oe://tasks` | Their tasks | as `GET /tasks` |
| `oe://watches` | What the Executive watches for them, as `GET /watchlist` lists it | someone on the roster |
| `oe://approvals` | What it may do on its own: the Approvals level and Your rules | as `GET /what-it-may-do` |
| `oe://people/roster` | The team on the roster (never contacts), as `GET /people` shows them | someone on the roster |
| `oe://memory/decisions` · `…/initiatives` · `…/advice` | Episodic memory; advice is the team's rows plus the caller's own | the principal |

The department level is read once, in the departments store (`department_level`, the level that applies from Approvals), and named once (`AuthorityLevel.label`), so the brief, the web app and this server always agree.

## Tools (capabilities)

| Tool | What it does | Annotations |
|---|---|---|
| `consult_specialist(specialist, query, context)` | Domain analysis from one of ten specialists, grounded in company knowledge. Stateless. | read-only, closed world |
| `search_knowledge(query)` | Retrieval over the curated knowledge base + indexed company docs | read-only, closed world |
| `list_workflows()` | Catalog of workflows and their inputs | read-only, closed world |
| `run_workflow(workflow, inputs)` | Runs one workflow as the person and returns its result | acts, open world |
| `answer_card(card_id, answer, reply)` | Approve, Skip or reply to a Needs you card | acts, open world |
| `ask_executive(message)` | One Executive answer, as the verified caller | acts, open world |
| `post_progress_update(topic, status, summary, ask, link, idempotency_key)` | Another agent's short progress update: stored, then sent to the founders' chat apps (see Progress updates below) | not read-only, not destructive, not idempotent, open world |

The ten specialists are cso, cfo, chro, gc, coo, cmo, cpo, sales, board_comms and triage. "Acts" is `readOnlyHint=False, destructiveHint=True, idempotentHint=False, openWorldHint=True`. A caller that resolves to no one reads and publishes no one's documents.

## An AI app's turn is the person's own

`ask_executive`, `answer_card` and `run_workflow` each run one Executive turn as the caller the API verified (`from_mcp_client`, `caller_person_id`). There is no separate tool list, header or switch for AI apps: the turn is offered what the web chat offers that person, and every step goes through the same three checks as every channel, in order: **Approvals** (Careful, Balanced or Hands-off), **Your rules**, and **In training**. A step that waits lands on a Needs you card. A caller who resolves to no one is an unrostered speaker, so everything they ask that sends or changes something waits for the owner.

- `answer_card` sends the same words the chat reads for a card ("Yes, approve card N.", "No, drop card N.", "About card N: …"), so the chat's own card checks decide.
- `run_workflow` sends "Run the <name> workflow with these inputs: …", so the chat's `run_workflow` tool and its checks decide.
- `answer_card` checks in code, before any model call, that the card is open and one the caller sees on Home (the alerts route's own rule). The turn then trusts that card only (`Session.answering_card`): `find_alerts` adds no other, so it can answer no other card.
- `run_workflow` takes only a workflow on `list_workflows`, with inputs checked against that workflow's input schema (unknown fields dropped). Every turn takes at most the web chat's 32,000 characters.
- Act as me needs a sign-in, as on the web chat: a request that only holds the shared secret never gets it.
- No History note or worked-out figure is learned from an AI app's text.
- Every audit row the turn writes carries `via`: the client's `clientInfo.name`, or "an AI app", and a card keeps it too.


Read-only turns are now only a host page's turn and a run queued for someone else (`schedule_tools.read_only_turn`).

## Progress updates (`post_progress_update`)

The one tool that stores and sends outside Approvals, whoever the caller is. The update is filed under the source its `x-source-token` header belongs to (`integrations.progress_sources`: the API holds only each token's sha256, in `PROGRESS_SOURCES`), so there is no source argument and the token stays out of model context and tool-call logs. With `BACKEND_SHARED_SECRET` set, the request must also have passed the shared-secret gate (`api/main.py` sets `request.state.shared_secret_ok`, read through `mcp_server.SHARED_SECRET_OK`, and nothing else reads it). An in-process call, a call with no HTTP request, the feature off (no source configured, a malformed `PROGRESS_SOURCES`, or a client slot or demo fixture live), a missing or unknown token, and a request that did not pass the gate all get the same fixed refusal, so it says nothing about which check failed.

Every rule lives in `integrations.progress_updates.submit`, which `POST /progress-updates` shares: a guard rejection comes back as `field: reason` (the field name truncated), the source's daily cap as an error, and a store failure, or a fixture, client-slot or sync write still running after a 10-second wait, as one fixed message, with nothing stored or sent. The result is `{id, stored, relay}`, `relay` either `accepted` or `duplicate`: whether a message went out is never returned, so a source cannot learn a founder's quiet hours or settings. Past the source's relay cap an update is stored but not sent, and each founder's next brief carries one notice that more are waiting. The content contract (no unpublished prices, personal data or credentials) is in the tool description; see Integrations for the guard, the relay and what the guard cannot catch.

Behind a shared secret an MCP source must hold `x-api-key` as well, and that secret opens the whole API (as a service, never the owner, with signed callers on). `POST /progress-updates` takes the source token alone, so it is the least-privilege path for a source that needs nothing else.

## Why prompt caching is unaffected

This path is parallel to chat. Resources are pure reads; `consult_specialist` delegates to the same `BaseAgent.analyze` that the chat path uses. An AI app's turn gets the same tool list as the person's web chat turn, so it shares that cached tool prefix. MCP *prompts* are skipped: OE workflows are server-executed orchestrations, not message templates. `post_progress_update` makes no model call, and a chat turn reads stored updates only in the user-turn `<briefing>` block.

## The `specialist` argument is resolved, not matched

The `specialist` value is **resolved** with the same `router.resolve_specialist_name` the chat path uses, so a re-cased or truncated name (`csO`, `cs`) reaches the intended specialist here exactly as it does in chat. An exact-membership check would have given external clients a stricter, divergent policy and would also have skipped the `routing_anomaly` audit row.

That tolerance has to be spelled in the **type hint**, not just in the handler. FastMCP builds a Pydantic model from the tool signature and validates arguments against it before the handler body runs, so while `specialist` was annotated as a bare `Literal` of the registry keys, `csO` was refused at the schema layer with a `literal_error` and the resolver never ran — the parity above was documented but not delivered. The parameter is therefore typed `str` with the roster attached as `json_schema_extra={"enum": …}`: clients still see the exact ten values in the advertised tool schema, *server-side* validation no longer rejects anything outside them, and the **raw** name is forwarded to `route_to_specialist`, which is where the correction and its `routing_anomaly` row are recorded. The tolerance is server-side only by design — the advertised schema still carries `enum`, so a client that validates outbound arguments against it will still refuse to send `csO` before the request leaves, which is the right behaviour for a client that can tell the name is wrong. What the widening buys is the case the resolver was written for: a *model* emitting a truncated name through a client that passes arguments straight through. Normalising at the validator boundary would have kept the enum too, but it would have erased the anomaly it exists to log. A name that genuinely resolves to nothing still raises `ValueError` (with the name truncated, since it is now unbounded text from an external client) rather than returning prose: an MCP caller is a program that wants an error, not a model that wants a recoverable `tool_result`.
